Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

Palantir Technologies has the highest price for its profit in its group of five large technology companies.
Its shares trade at 105.7 times its past year's profit, the top figure in the group. It also has the fastest sales growth, 87.1% in the four quarters to September 30, 2026. So are you overpaying, or paying for growth no rival in the group delivers?

We looked at this group on Tuesday. For that piece, see Is Palantir Stock Priced Right Against Its Rivals? This one asks what the extra price pays for.

How much more does Palantir cost than its rivals?

The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, is the share price divided by a year's profit per share. A higher P/E means you pay more for each dollar the company earns.

Microsoft makes the sharpest contrast. Its P/E is 25.8. It keeps a slightly larger share of sales as operating profit, 47.1% against Palantir's 45.6%. That share is the operating margin. But Microsoft grew sales 17.9%, far below Palantir's 87.1%.

Palantir pays no dividend. So everything a holder earns has to come from the share price, which closed at $161.18 on Tuesday.

Palantir sends its owners no cash, so at $161 a share any gain must come from the price rising. If you need your savings to cover the bills each month, this stock will not send you a check while you hold it.. Every other peer sits below Palantir on both price and growth. So the highest P/E comes with the highest growth. On margin, Palantir ranks second of five.

Bill Ackman, George Soros and 5 Other Famous Investors Own Microsoft. Here's Who Bought and Sold Recently ©Natee Meepian's Images and Mike Marchetti from baseimage via Canva
Key Takeaways

Seven famous investors held Microsoft on Sept. 30. Dan Loeb's Third Point and Peter Thiel's Thiel Macro opened new stakes, while Bill Ackman's Pershing Square and George Soros' fund each cut about a third of theirs.

AI spending has cut into Microsoft's cash, and analysts expect $32.0 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2027, down from $67.0 billion in fiscal 2026. Amazon's spending has already turned its free cash flow negative.

Analysts expect earnings per share to grow 16% in fiscal 2027 and 21% in fiscal 2028, and the stock trades at 24x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 29x.

The numbers side with the buyers. The December-quarter report in late January will show whether the cash holds up.

Seven famous investors held Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) at the end of September, according to their 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed from Nov. 6 to Nov. 16. They didn't agree on it: Bill Ackman's Pershing Square and George Soros' Soros Fund Management cut their stakes, while Dan Loeb's Third Point and Peter Thiel's Thiel Macro bought in.

The split comes as Microsoft's AI build-out eats into its cash. Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) has the same problem, and its free cash flow has already gone negative.

Ackman and Soros sold, Loeb and Thiel bought

The biggest move in dollars was a sale. Pershing Square cut its stake 35% in the third quarter, to 4.06 million shares from 6.21 million, which is about $1.10 billion of stock at quarter-end prices. Even after the cut, Microsoft was still Pershing's fourth-largest holding at $2.08 billion, or 6.8% of its 13F stocks. Soros Fund Management cut 36%, to 122,166 shares, and what's left is 1.0% of its 13F stocks.

On the buying side, Third Point opened a 450,000-share stake worth $231 million. That made Microsoft its sixth-largest holding, at 5.1% of its 13F stocks. Thiel Macro's new stake is a token one: 2,000 shares worth about $1 million, or 0.2% of the $460 million its 13F holds in US stocks.

TIKR tracks 58 analysts on Microsoft. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Microsoft, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Microsoft's Analyst Ratings

Everyone else mostly held on

The other three holders barely moved. Ken Fisher's Fisher Investments is by far the biggest of the seven, with 27.14 million shares worth $13.92 billion on Sept. 30 after adding 2%. Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital trimmed 7% and still held $607 million, its eighth-largest position. Cathie Wood's ARK Invest cut 8%, to just 5,693 shares. Microsoft stock is down 3% from its quarter-end price, so it has barely moved since the filings' snapshot.

Salesforce (CRM) stock looks mispriced after the recent software sell-off, driven by fears that artificial intelligence (AI) will disrupt traditional enterprise software. The customer relationship management software provider enters this stretch from a position of financial strength, having generated $14.4 billion in free cash flow in Fiscal 2026. In the company's second-quarter Fiscal 2027 earnings release in August 2026, Chair and CEO Marc Benioff addressed the AI opportunity and pushed back against the disruption narrative, stating, "AI is delivering value across every layer of our platform."

I think investors are overlooking how little physical investment Salesforce needs to pursue that opportunity, with capex projected at roughly 1.5% of revenue in Fiscal 2027. Rather than being replaced, its software can become more useful and more embedded as enterprises adopt autonomous AI agents across workflows, in my view. Yet the market seems far more concerned about disruption. Ahead of the company's third-quarter earnings report on December 2, I rate CRM a Buy.

AI Exposure Without the Infrastructure Bill

What I like about Salesforce is that it offers AI exposure without the huge infrastructure bill. Now, Monday's rally following Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia (NVDA) lifted CRM 2.7%. Yet shares remain roughly 26% below their August post-earnings level. Investors have sold software alongside companies facing enormous graphics processing unit (GPU) and power commitments, but Salesforce's spending requirements look very different.

For context, Salesforce's Fiscal 2026 operating cash flow reached $15 billion, with FCF of $14.4 billion. However, physical capex consumed only about 4% of operating cash. Its most recent Q2 FY27 results repeated the pattern, with $1.3 billion of operating cash and $1.1 billion of FCF.

We are seeing that Salesforce can keep developing Agentforce without committing tens of billions to new data centers. That leaves more flexibility for shareholder-friendly capital allocation, including ongoing share buybacks and its quarterly dividend. I find that appealing, especially as infrastructure financing has become such a concern elsewhere in the technology sector.

Okta (OKTA) stock is 29.3% under the highest close it set in February 2021. $10,000 put into Okta at its first close in April 2017 was worth $87,741 on Monday, before dividends. The same money in the S&P 500 grew to $30,724, also before dividends. In hindsight it looks like an easy hold. How many times do you think Okta fell 20% or more on the way?

The deepest fall is also the latest. Okta dropped 84.6% from February 2021 to November 2022. The S&P 500 lost 4.2% over the same dates, before dividends. As of Monday, Okta has still not closed above that 2021 high, 69.3 months later.

A wait that long is hard for anyone who needs income from their savings, and Okta makes no regular cash payout to holders. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

What Was It Like To Hold Okta Through A Fall?

Take the fall that began in July 2019. Okta slid for 7.7 months. At the low in March 2020, it was down 31.6%. It climbed back above its old high in about a month.

A holder in March 2020 saw only the loss, with no way to know when it would end. The 2018 and 2019 falls both ended above their old highs. Nobody in the middle of one knew that.

Was Something Wrong With Okta's Business?

Okta sells what its management calls "workforce identity and customer identity platforms." That is software that checks who may sign in to a company's systems.

In the deepest fall, twelve-month sales rose 107.3% between the high and the low. Part of that rise was bought: Okta took over another company in mid-2021. But the losses widened. The operating loss, what running the business cost beyond its sales, went from 24.4% of sales to 49.5%.

In the 2019 fall, sales rose 32.9% and the operating loss held near a third of sales. The business held up then. In the deepest fall, Okta lost more on each dollar of sales.

What Selling Okta Stock Would Have Cost

Okta is up 358.2% since its November 2022 low. Anyone who sold there missed all of it. Okta is still 29.3% under its February 2021 high. For more on the wait for that high, see Is Okta Stock Worth The Wait?
